canberra.title: ‘Strategy is working’: Steel highlights cash and debt improvements but Budget deficit is $55 million worse
canberra.snippet: ACT Treasurer Chris Steel is touting an early return to cash operating balance and a small dip in forecast net debt as evidence that the ...
canberra.content:
Treasurer Chris Steel MLA says budget repair is on track. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

ACT Treasurer Chris Steel is touting an early return to cash operating balance and a small dip in forecast net debt as evidence that the ACT Government’s budget repair strategy is working, despite an increase in the deficit.

The 2025-26 Interim Budget Result shows a $55 million deterioration in the deficit to $556.6 million, due to lower tax revenue and higher spending.

But the Net Operating Cash Balance was a surplus of $74.9 million, an improvement of $255.5 million compared to the 2025-26 estimated deficit of $180.6 million.

This was a year earlier than anticipated in this year’s Budget, driven mainly by a strong Australian dollar, which delivered greater hedging gains from foreign exchange rate movements, and by lower spending on supplies and services.

Net debt, at $10,976.1 million, will be $113.4 million lower than the 2025-26 estimated outcome of $11,089.5 million published at the 2026-27 Budget, due to higher cash and investments.

But net debt increased by $1825.4 million compared to 2024-25, mainly due to greater borrowing for the Territory’s infrastructure program and prevailing cash flow requirements, partially offset by higher cash and investment balances.

Mr Steel said the updated Budget figures showed that the government’s commitment to improving the Territory’s fiscal position was working.

“Achieving a cash operating surplus earlier than expected is an important milestone in delivering on our fiscal strategy to improve the Budget bottom line, while ensuring Canberrans can benefit from high-quality local services,” he said.

“With a better Budget position and lower than estimated net debt, the government is delivering responsive and responsible fiscal management.”

But Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton said only the ACT Labor Government would claim success from failure. Revenue fell $110 million short of budget.

Mr Parton said expenses blew out by $83 million, the UPF net operating balance (revenue minus expenses) is $193 million worse than promised, and net debt surged by more than $1.8 billion in a single year.

“If Treasurer Steel still says the budget is ‘under control’, how does he explain this? This is not fiscal management. It is fiscal freefall, and Canberra taxpayers are paying the price,” he said.

Revenue was $29.5 million less than the 2025-26 estimate of $8846.1 million, due to lower payroll tax as a result of the Commonwealth’s reduced use of consultants and less stamp duty amid the property market downturn.

There was also lower revenue from Suburban Land Agency land sales, but this was offset by lower SLA infrastructure spending and higher Commonwealth grants.

Government spending was $39.1 million higher than expected, at $9653.2 million.

This was due to higher insurance claims from an increased number of historical abuse claims, and higher than expected medical negligence and public liability claims.

The government spent more on staff than expected, mainly due to the recruitment of additional clinical staff at Canberra Health Services, higher employee entitlements such as annual leave, overtime, and allowances, and the in-house recruitment of contracted staff.

This was partially offset by less reliance on contracted services, and rescheduled procurements and revised project timelines.

canberra.title: Stranger’s alleged attack on two children reveals failures by police, mental health system
canberra.snippet: The distressing alleged assault of two boys inside a Canberra mall has revealed an intersection between the failings of police and the me...
canberra.content:
Two children were allegedly assaulted at Westfield Belconnen on Friday (14 August), which has seen charges laid against an 18-year-old man. Photo: Westfield Belconnen Facebook, Michelle Kroll, Albert McKnight.

The distressing alleged assault of two boys inside a Canberra mall has revealed an intersection between the failings of police and the mental health support system, as well as the need to protect the community from a “vulnerable” man who is accused of being fixated on children.

The two boys, aged two and four, were with their mother at Westfield Belconnen on Friday (14 August) when a stranger allegedly attacked them.

The two-year-old was apparently left with a broken nose.

Bystanders and security apparently restrained the 18-year-old man alleged to have attacked them. But he was released because, despite receiving Triple Zero calls about the incident, ACT Policing did not send officers to the scene, nor did they speak to the children’s family for some time.

This delayed response ultimately resulted in a public apology.

“We did receive calls about the incident at the time, but police didn’t attend,” ACT Policing’s Deputy Chief Police Officer Richard Chin told the ABC on Monday (17 August).

“Our response to the family at that time and after the incident wasn’t in line with our own expectations as ACT Policing, and certainly wasn’t in line with what the community would expect from us.

“We met with and apologised unreservedly to the family involved … We absolutely should have done better.”

Deputy Chief Police Officer Chin said a review was underway to understand what occurred, but he admitted police “simply didn’t prioritise this matter appropriately”.

The 18-year-old man, whose name has been legally suppressed, was arrested over the weekend and faced the ACT Magistrates Court later on Monday charged with two counts of assault.

“Hey Mum, I want to come home on bail. I’m really upset,” he told his mother, who was soon seen crying in the courtroom gallery.

The court heard the man has previously been accused of attacking three children in 2025. He is alleged to have assaulted a three-year-old in May, another three-year-old in June, then a six-year-old in August.

Chief Magistrate Louise Taylor said the allegations demonstrated a “pattern of conduct”.

“It’s impulsive, it’s dangerous, it’s frightening, and ultimately, it’s resulting in significant injuries to members of the community made particularly vulnerable by their age and circumstances,” she said.

Prosecutor Marcus Dyason opposed the man’s bail application, saying he was alleged to have engaged in conduct that could result in a vigilante-style response.

Chief Magistrate Taylor agreed, saying members of the community may not know the man’s vulnerabilities, but it would be very difficult for them when confronted with the sight of children being assaulted.

“It’s a very dangerous and volatile situation that’s being created,” she said.

“For whatever reason, there is a fixation on little people, which only elevates the risk that he poses.”

Chief Magistrate Taylor accepted he had several very significant challenges, but she questioned how he was able to go to the mall by himself on Friday when he was supposed to be living in 24-hour supported accommodation.

The chief magistrate said if he was allowed to go into the community on his own without support, that would be “frankly preposterous” in light of his recent history.

His lawyer, Legal Aid’s Gillian Bilton, said he was a “very, very vulnerable young man”.

She said there had recently been disengagement from his support officer, he had lost the support of his occupational therapist, and there had been a reduction in his ability to access a behavioural therapist. He hadn’t seen someone in the latter profession for about two months.

Ms Bilton said there had been “a gap” in his care and, in particular, an “administrative oversight” by the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

When court was adjourned for a short time so Ms Bilton could make further inquiries, the man tried to run away from the custodial officers guarding him. The officers grabbed him while he was still inside the courtroom, and he screamed, “I want to go home”.

Chief Magistrate Taylor ultimately said the risk that the man would endanger members of the community was too high and remanded him in custody. However, she granted leave for the lawyers to relist the matter at short notice to revisit the question of bail.

She marked the man as a prisoner at risk, adjourned to September and made a non-publication order on his name, which prevents it from being reported.

canberra.title: ‘Labor Party gun grab’: Riverina takes aim at 274,000-firearm buyback scheme
canberra.snippet: Riverina firearm owners and political leaders have hit out at the Federal and NSW governments’ new gun buyback, accusing Labor of forcing...
canberra.content:
Cootamundra MP Steph Cooke, seen here at the Cowra Gun Club, has called on the NSW Government to rethink its buyback scheme. Photo: Steph Cooke/Facebook.

Riverina firearm owners and political leaders have hit out at the Federal and NSW governments’ new gun buyback, accusing Labor of forcing law-abiding shooters to hand over firearms for less than they are worth while wasting taxpayers’ money on a scheme they say won’t improve community safety.

The scheme follows the deadly antisemitic terrorist attack at Bondi Beach late last year, which killed 15 people and prompted governments to tighten gun laws and introduce a national firearms buyback.

Up to 274,000 registered firearms across NSW could be affected by new ownership limits and firearm reclassifications, with the government beginning to buy back guns on 2 November.

Griffith Sporting Shooters Association president Warren Brown said the scheme would not make communities safer.

“It’s just a Labor Party Gun grab,” he said.

“It’s placing the blame on law-abiding firearm users who are completely innocent, instead of looking at immigration vetting and the administration of the NSW Firearms Registry,” he said.

“We have laws in place – had they been followed, this tragedy never would have happened.”

New NSW laws generally limit individual licence holders to 10 firearms, depending on their genuine reason for owning them. They also prohibit some firearms, including belt-fed firearms, while other types have been moved into more restricted categories.

Those affected can surrender eligible firearms to the government in return for compensation.

Under the first phase of the buyback, the government will pay fixed amounts including $600 for a rimfire rifle, $1000 for a centrefire rifle and $650 for a single-barrel shotgun.

A second phase, beginning in early 2027, will provide compensation for eligible higher-value firearms priced at more than $3000, capped at $10,000 per firearm.

Mr Brown, 82, has been a sporting shooter for more than six decades and has built up an extensive firearms collection.

He said he would now have to surrender many of his firearms and said many gun owners will be left out of pocket.

“The government will pay $650 for a single-barrelled shotgun. That might be what you pay for a cheaper model, but a lot of people would’ve paid a lot more than that.

“They’ll be a maximum price paid of $10,000, but I know colleagues in Griffith who have shotguns worth up to $30,000.”

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese defended the reforms, saying they were necessary to improve community safety.

“We must do everything we can to make sure the antisemitic terrorist attack in Bondi doesn’t happen again. That includes meaningful nationwide gun reform,” Mr Albanese said.

“I thank the NSW Government for their collaboration as we work to take guns off our streets in order to better protect Australians.”

But Mr Brown said the hundreds of millions being spent on the buybacks could be better directed.

“It’s a total waste of money. They should spend that money on tackling illegal crime and unregistered firearms,” he said.

“The pollies say they want to take guns ‘off the street’. Our guns aren’t on the streets, they’re safely locked up.

“When was the last time you heard about an accident at a shooting club? But every second night, you hear about someone in Melbourne or Sydney being shot by a criminal. These laws will do nothing to prevent that.”

Cam Croke is another law-abiding firearm user who may be affected. Photo: supplied.

NSW and the Commonwealth will split the cost of the buyback 50:50, with the Commonwealth funding the destruction of surrendered firearms.

The government has not yet released a total cost estimate for the scheme.

Cootamundra Nationals MP Steph Cooke said she also opposed it.

“I stand with the thousands of licensed firearms owners across the Cootamundra electorate and the dealers who support them,” she said.

“They include farmers, sporting and recreational shooters, hunters, pest controllers, small business owners and employees who have followed the law, yet are being punished through no fault of their own.

“I believe the right thing to do is reverse Labor’s rushed and defective December 2025 firearms laws and return to the strict, workable legislative framework NSW had before Bondi. I will keep fighting for that.”

The scheme will also provide grants of up to $25,000 to eligible firearms businesses and dealers to help them adjust to the new laws.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Welcome to the world of darkness where harpies appear as the prophets of doom
canberra.snippet: In Greek and Roman mythology, harpies were half-bird, half-human creatures that personified destructive storm spirits. They were also kno...
canberra.content:
17 August 2026

Start the conversation

Judith Nangala Crispin, Off the South Coast, where Christmas tourist traffic threads the Kings Highway, and stops for no reason, not for bird or fallen roo—the ocean gathers up Brendan, at the edge of water, remakes his shattered hind leg and broken tail, his heart..., 120 x 91cm Photo: Grainger Gallery.

In Greek and Roman mythology, harpies were half-bird, half-human creatures that personified destructive storm spirits. They were also known as the hounds of Zeus. They were human vultures that in art frequently possessed beautiful, seductive female faces.

Judith Nangala Crispin is a First Nations artist, poet and environmentalist living near Braidwood, who for many years has worked with roadkill and innovative cameraless photographic techniques.

Stephen Harrison is another local, multifaceted artist who, for decades, has pursued the dark side of the landscape, with roaming thylacines, deserted lighthouses and the gothic architecture of Prague.

Crispin and Harrison together create a world of darkness in which harpies roam, reason gives way to surreal invention, and we are constantly reminded that our last hope for saving the world has passed and that we are now confronting inevitable global destruction and despair.

It is a world that the great Dante once described as the place where “the repellent harpies make their nests” from where they make their “dire announcements of the coming woe”.

Dante describes the harpies: “They have broad wings, with razor-sharp talons and a human neck and face, clawed feet and swollen, feathered bellies; they caw their lamentations in the eerie trees.”

Judith Nangala Crispin, The insects are leaving us, 100 x 61cm. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

Of the many exhibitions that Crispin has held in recent years, this one has a strong, deliberately religious character.

In some instances, her pieces have appropriated the forms of the painted altarpieces of Renaissance and Baroque masters, including Peter Paul Rubens, except the imagery is not devoted to the Godhead, the Virgin or the saints of the church, but to nature. It is to the sacrificed animals and insects who are now perishing in the landscape around us.

Take, for example, her metre-high panel, The Insects Are Leaving Us. If you pause and enter the work, there is a testimony to a great exodus of insects disappearing as a stream of tiny ghost-like beings into a heavenly direction.

Although the piece has an immediate impact, when you pause to examine it for a few minutes, the full richness of the tapestry of vision gradually reveals itself to us. In many of the pieces, collaged elements add glitter and texture to the surface.

Judith Nangala Crispin, I dreamed of spiders—a great hierarchy of limbs and fangs, stretching from the earth into the sky, and thousands of tiny insects climbed them, skittering over those huge arachnid forms, up and up, until they too were lost in blinding light, 150 x 59cm. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

In another piece, my favourite at the exhibition and shaped like a Baroque dissolving ceiling about one-and-a-half metres across, the poetic title leads us into the work, I dreamed of spiders—a great hierarchy of limbs and fangs, stretching from the earth into the sky, and thousands of tiny insects climbed them, skittering over those huge arachnid forms, up and up, until they too were lost in blinding light. The denuding of our environment of insects and spiders is a prelude to the denuding of our planet of humans.

There are also a number of her more traditional roadkill images. One of the most powerful is titled Off the South Coast, where Christmas tourist traffic threads the Kings Highway, and stops for no reason, not for bird or fallen roo—the ocean gathers up Brendan, at the edge of water, remakes his shattered hind leg and broken tail, his heart…. It is a powerful manifestation as a monument to our sacrificed wildlife.

Stephen Harrison, Death Hugging a Tower, 54 x 20 x 12cm, clay and paint. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

Stephen Harrison’s contribution to the exhibition consists mainly of three-dimensional pieces in bronze, lead, clay and glass, largely professionally cast by Nick Stranks.

If Crispin’s images resemble altarpieces, Harrison’s are more like holy relics with symbolic and allegorical forms. His pieces have a haunting simplicity, such as Death hugging a tower or the wonderfully expressive, The harpy poet, made out of bronze and glass.

Stephen Harrison, The Poet Harpy, 41 x 32 x 32 cm, bronze and glass. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

They are essentially table-sized sculptures that tackle the theme of our lost ecology, as in his wonderful bronze-and-lead piece, The thylacine dreamt of hunting.

All of his pieces bear the expressive mark of being made by the human hand, and no matter how absurd they initially appear, they bear testimony to a vanishing past and the prophecy that the future is something dark and inevitable.

Stephen Harrison, The Thylacine Dreamt of Hunting, 28 x 29 x 20cm, bronze and lead. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

Judith Nangala Crispin and Stephen Harrison: Afternoon of harpies is now open at the Grainger Gallery, 1/34 Geelong St, Fyshwick, until 30 August. It’s open Thursday to Sunday, 11 am to 4 pm.

canberra.title: Generous Canberrans to take a dip in Lake Burley Griffin for 40 years of Daffodil Day
canberra.snippet: To mark 40 years of Daffodil Day, Cancer Council ACT is calling on the community to take a dip into the chilly waters of Lake Burley Grif...
canberra.content:
17 August 2026

Start the conversation

Cancer Council ACT is launching Daffodil Day 2026 with a special dip in Lake Burley Griffin. Photo: Cancer Council ACT.

To mark 40 years of Daffodil Day, Cancer Council ACT is calling on the community to take a dip into the chilly waters of Lake Burley Griffin to raise money for local cancer research.

All members of the Canberra community are invited to take the plunge alongside players from the ACT Brumbies at The Red Shed at 6:30 am on Wednesday (19 August) to officially kick off Daffodil Day.

Daffodil Day is an iconic annual fundraising event held by the Cancer Council, with businesses often hosting morning teas and lunches and accepting donations from participants.

In Australia, almost one in two people will be diagnosed with cancer before the age of 85, with an estimated 170,000-plus Australians diagnosed with cancer last year, more than 466 per day.

It is also estimated around 53,500 Australians died from cancer in 2025.

Cancer Council ACT CEO Verity Hawkins said Cancer Council ACT and the events it is holding as part of Daffodil Day are vital in helping reduce these numbers.

“The impact of that community support has been extraordinary,” Ms Hawkins said.

“In 1986, the five-year cancer survival rate was approximately 46 per cent. Today it has risen to 72 per cent, meaning nearly three out of four Australians diagnosed with cancer will survive at least five years after diagnosis.

“For 40 years, Daffodil Day has given our community a way to stand together against cancer. Every bunch of daffodils sold, every yellow morning tea, every cold dip, and every dollar donated funds vital research that is happening right now, right here in Canberra.

“We’ve made remarkable progress over the past four decades, but there’s still more work to do.

“Daffodil Day reminds us that when our community comes together, we can help fund better treatments, better outcomes and more hope for families facing cancer.”

Ms Hawkins said the dip is a special way of building excitement for this year’s Daffodil Day while also providing a memorable experience for people to enjoy.

”Every participant plays an important part in helping us create a future free from cancer,” she said.

“Whether you’re taking the plunge, making a donation or cheering from the sidelines, every person who gets involved is helping fund local life-saving cancer research. Together, we’re growing hope for the future.

“The Daffodil Day community dip is open to all ages, with participants encouraged to invite friends, family and colleagues to join them for a memorable morning dip supporting an important cause.”

To find out more about Daffodil Day or register for the Burley Griffin dip, visit Cancer Council ACT.

australia.title: Labor pledges opt-out register for online gambling ads as Pocock calls out shortfalls in government’s bill
australia.snippet: The new measure falls short of calls for gambling ads to move to an opt-in model, or for an outright ban Follow our Australia news live b...
australia.content:
The Labor government has pledged a new single-service opt-out register for gambling ads – an idea similar to the Do Not Call register for spam calls – as part of amendments to its wagering ad bill, as well as restrictions on inducements and limiting commissions for agents.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, has also confirmed gambling companies will face a new levy to pay for the register, a beefed-up measure to curb wagering ads, after concerns were raised through a Senate inquiry that people would struggle to find or complete individual opt-out options on each online service.

The measure falls short of calls from some, including Labor and Liberal MPs, for an “opt-in” model for gambling ads, or for a complete ban on online advertising.

But despite Labor’s hopes to speed its gambling changes through parliament this week, members of the Coalition, Greens and independent David Pocock savaged the government’s bills in scathing comments in a Senate inquiry report, calling out “deficiencies” in curbing ads.

The Albanese government’s gambling reforms are expected to proceed quickly through parliament this week, with Labor sources saying they hoped the changes contained in two separate bills would pass both houses before the end of Thursday.

Despite the Senate report, government sources remain confident of an imminent agreement with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, after multiple meetings with Anthony Albanese last week – even though the Coalition has not yet publicly committed to supporting the package.

While a further raft of amendments to the bill are likely to be outlined on Tuesday, Wells on Monday introduced a third bill setting out changes the government proposes to make to its own legislation.

The bill’s explanatory memorandum says the government’s plans include “restricting the use of inducements by licensed interactive wagering service providers”, as well as plans to prohibit “inducement-based direct marketing and social media advertising to certain customers”. It also aims to restrict “attempts to obtain consent to receive such marketing [and] prohibits certain commission-based referral arrangements”.

“The government has listened carefully to the evidence presented during the recent Senate inquiry and through ongoing stakeholder engagement. We are particularly concerned by evidence about wagering inducements and the role these practices can play in encouraging gambling and exacerbating gambling-related harm,” Wells told parliament in introducing the new bill.

The new focus on wagering inducements – which were not addressed in Labor’s initial legislation – came after allegations in explosive parliamentary hearings this month that wagering companies provided illegal drugs and access to sex workers to keep problem gamblers betting. Betting giants Sportsbet and Tabcorp have said there is no evidence to substantiate these claims.

A major change contained in Monday’s third bill is a new “Wagering Advertising Opt-out Register”. While neither Wells’ speech nor the explanatory memorandum explains exactly how this would work, the explanation says it would be “a single mechanism through which individuals may opt out of receiving wagering advertising from online content service providers”.

Wells told parliament that the register would “provide Australians with a ‘one-stop shop’ to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms”. It will be administered and established by the Australian Communications and Media Authority.

Guardian Australia is seeking information about how the register would operate. Government sources conceded it would be a complex measure, with more details yet to be confirmed. It is unclear whether the register would be ready in time for 1 January 2027, when many measures in the government’s wagering changes come into force.

Labor’s initial bill had stopped short of enacting a full ban on wagering ads online, as recommended by Peta Murphy’s landmark 2023 parliamentary report, in favour of establishing a “triple lock” system for ads to be shown online; that online ads could only be shown to users who are logged in and aged over 18, and provided with an opt-out feature.

But gambling harm advocates and critics of Labor’s bill had criticised this system, saying existing opt-out features on streaming services or social media platforms were often hard to find online, and that only a tiny percentage of users had made use of those features.

Pocock, in his comments for the Senate report, pointed out that SBS had told the committee only 130,000 of the 15 million account holders for its on-demand streaming service had opted-out of gambling ads.

The government’s new proposal for a single opt-out register is a compromise to provide an easier avenue for opting out of ads, without enacting a full ban or switching to an opt-in.

“This bill enables the ACMA to recover the costs of those activities through a levy imposed on licensed interactive wagering service providers. It is appropriate that the wagering industry, rather than taxpayers, bears the costs of regulating these activities,” Wells said.

In the Senate report, Labor senators recommended the bill pass. But senator Sarah Hanson-Young said the Greens would not support the bill in its current form, calling again for a full online ad ban, a national gambling regulator and the banning of all inducements.

Pocock said the bill would “not break the connection between sport and gambling”, which has been one of Labor’s stated aims, and would not minimise children’s exposure to wagering ads. He also questioned whether the government had put the interests of sporting codes and wagering companies above public health concerns around gambling harm.

Coalition senators Sarah Henderson and Dean Smith wrote that “the vast majority of Australians” who gamble “do so responsibly”. But while they also praised the “important role that the wagering and related industries play”, they too raised concerns about inducements and the targeting of children.

“The government has had more than three years to get this right. Regrettably, this bill falls well short.”

australia.title: ‘Our new normal’: how marine heatwaves affect life in British seas
australia.snippet: As warming seas push native species to cooler waters farther north, once-rare visitors have become more common ‘It sounds silly but I tho...
australia.content:
‘It sounds silly but I thought it was a person in the water waving,” says Kurt Lander, skipper of the Yellowfin charter boat, based out of Brighton. But when he grabbed his binoculars, he realised the fluttering movement he had noticed in the middle of the Channel shipping lane was a pair of sunfish.

The huge fish were lying on their sides and flapping their fins. “Apparently, they do it as a visual attraction to birds,” he says. “They’re trying to get the birds to eat the parasites off them.”

Lander has seen the huge fish with their unusual round bodies before. But the difference is that those that he spotted this year are part of a surge in sightings of the species off British shores this summer, probably as a result of a marine heatwave.

Marine heatwaves usually follow long hot spells on land as seas also warm. Last year was labelled “exceptional” by the Met Office, with some parts of British waters seeing heatwave conditions for three-quarters of the year, and 2026 is already showing more of the same.

The extraordinary temperatures are causing shifts in marine life far beyond an increase in sunfish. Some species are moving away from warmer waters, other “invaders” are appearing for the first time around Britain’s coastline, while some marine life is dying off under the rays of the sun.

Lander notices the change in the species of fish he now lands. “I used to catch at least a couple of hundred cod a year,” he says. Now, bringing in cod is rare. If he catches any, he adds, “it’s probably about one or two a year in the summer.”

Colder water species are just nowhere to be seen off the southern coastline, says Dr Zoe Jacobs, a senior researcher at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. Shifting their range to cooler seas farther north, they are now thriving in Scotland. “Temporarily or permanently, we don’t know,” she says.

Meanwhile, Lander is catching more warm-water fish, such as bass, comber and triggerfish. According to last year’s State of the South-West Seas report, other species found in warmer waters – such as sardines and anchovies – are also doing well.

Gio Reale, a diver based in the Cornish port of Falmouth, says: “Small water temperature changes have such big effects on marine life.” It has been weeks since he last saw his favourite shark species: the small spotted catshark (also called the lesser-spotted dogfish). These small sharks – which grow no bigger than a metre and are spattered with delicate freckles – prefer water temperatures of about 16-17C (61-63F).

“This summer, like every day, the water has been about 20C,” he says, adding that he thinks the sharks may have moved into deeper, cooler waters, replicating the way they behave in the Mediterranean.

These sharks may be missing but common octopuses have arrived in force since January last year, when warmer waters in Devon and Cornwall created perfect conditions for them. This species is native to the UK but not usually seen.

The bloom caused issues for some crab and lobster fishers. “Everyone’s complaining, ‘oh, they’re taking all our crabs’,” says Reale. “But obviously, for the octopus, that’s just a really easy meal. You can just get into a trap where the crabs can’t go anywhere and eat them.”

Some boats have switched to targeting the now-abundant octopuses, with catches soaring in 2026. The octopuses also provide food for predators, which could explain an increase in sightings of summer visitors such as Risso’s dolphins.

As sea swimmers know, warmer waters also bring jellyfish – another food source. But these blooms “have high and low years”, says Jacobs, and interpreting sightings can be tricky: reports may increase simply because more people are at the beach.

Seeing lots of native moon, compass and barrel jellyfish is normal for summer. However, the arrival of more mauve stingers from the Mediterranean would be “a different story”, she says. “That might well be due to the warming.”

Warmer waters can bring new species altogether. A few smalltooth sand tiger sharks – an “exceptionally rare visitor” in local waters – have washed up on UK beaches in recent years, and hair curler sea slugs , usually found in the Caribbean and Mediterranean, were first recorded in 2025.

Some outsiders can cause problems for native animals. For example, scientists are watching a newly arrived sea squirt, called Didemnum pseudovexillum, closely. It is almost identical to another invader called the carpet sea squirt (Didemnum vexillum) that can smother the seabed, but they do not yet know if this new sea squirt will cause similar damage.

Elsewhere in the world, extreme marine heatwaves have caused extensive loss of seagrass and kelp in countries including Australia and the US. “Huge areas have just been completely wiped out, and they’ve not returned,” says Jacobs.

Chris Williams, founder of the volunteer-run Hastings Kelp Project, is worried. The UK may have lost about 92% of its seagrass meadows since the 1930s. Exactly how much kelp has vanished is unclear but, in Sussex, it could be more than 96%.

And this is hidden under the sea. “You don’t see a degrading kelp forest from the land like you might see a woodland burning down or dying off because of the temperatures,” he says.

Kelp prefers waters of about 8-12C and even Williams’s controlled laboratory is struggling. “Because of the heatwave, our chillers in the lab haven’t been able to keep the tanks below 12C,” he says.

His kelp is growing but he thinks this is because he can control other variables, such as lighting.

Seagrass and kelp provide vital habitats for many animals, protect shorelines from erosion and flooding, and store carbon, which is why Williams hopes to grow kelp that can withstand warmer seas. The Seagrass Ocean Rescue project similarly aims to restore 15% of UK seagrass meadows by 2030.

Warmer waters can also trigger harmful algal blooms, which can harbour nasty pathogens that make animals and people extremely sick. In the Bay of Biscay, the authorities closed beaches to protect swimmers. While the same thing could happen here, our infrastructure is not yet set up for such closures, says Jacobs. “We’re just not ready,” she says.

The impact of repeated heatwaves on fisheries may take a couple of years to become apparent because, even if adults survived the elevated temperatures, eggs and juveniles may have been affected. And experts do not know if the cold-water fishes that moved north will return after the heatwaves end.

“It might be that our cod and mackerel fisheries are done,” says Jacobs. But southern vessels could pivot to catch warmer water species, such as triggerfish, while Scotland benefits from the cod’s shift in its range.

Marine heatwaves are not new but climate breakdown is causing them to hit with increasing frequency and severity. “I’m starting to call it our new normal because we seem to be getting hit by them in successive years,” says Jacobs.

As greenhouse gases emitted from burning fossil fuels push up baseline temperatures, “the extreme is just going to be more extreme”, she says.

australia.title: Canavan and Joyce attend anti-abortion rally and back controversial bill – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Labor pledges opt-out register for online gambling ads akin to Do Not Call register for spam calls Get our breaki...
australia.content:
Key events
